q: what was the dancing plague of 1518
a: The Dancing Plague of 1518 was a bizarre event in Strasbourg (then part of the Holy Roman Empire) in July 1518, when a woman named Frau Troffea began dancing feverishly in the street. Within a month, hundreds of others had joined her, dancing uncontrollably for days without rest. Many died from heart attacks, strokes, or exhaustion. Contemporary accounts mention 15 deaths per day at the peak. The cause remains debated by historians and medical researchers. Leading theories include mass psychogenic illness (mass hysteria) triggered by extreme stress and superstitious beliefs, ergot poisoning (fungus on rye bread that causes convulsions and hallucinations similar to LSD), or a combination of both. The event was well-documented by contemporary sources including physicians, city records, and religious authorities. City officials eventually responded by hiring musicians to accompany the dancers, building a stage, and even shipping afflicted dancers to a shrine for St. Vitus. The dancing eventually subsided after several weeks. Similar dancing plagues occurred elsewhere in Europe during the same period, though none as large as the 1518 Strasbourg event.
